g.passage: Mangoes, mostly, though the orchard outside Surabaya had long ago given up deciding. Arisa counted eleven trees still standing and two that had lain down sometime before the rains. Thuy said the fallen ones were resting. Arisa said they were firewood with good manners. They walked the rows the way they had as girls, kicking husks, naming the trees after teachers they had disliked. At the gate Arisa took a parcel from her bag: the brass bell Thuy had mailed to her new flat in Jakarta, still in its paper, the knot untouched. Thuy looked at the knot, not at the bell. She did not ask why. Arisa tied the parcel to the lowest branch of the eleventh tree, where the wind could reach it, and stepped back. They waited. When it rang once, faintly, Thuy reached up and tightened the knot so it would hold through the season.

g.passage: Three rules for the salt pans, Aoife had told the squad on the first morning: hats on, water every hour, no running where the crust is thin. Lanying had broken the third rule once, two years ago today, and had not played a full match since. Now she sat on the cooler with her knee strapped, timing the others' sprints with a stopwatch that ran four seconds slow. Aoife did not correct it. She read the numbers aloud as given and wrote them on her clipboard in neat columns. At noon the team left for lunch in the van. Aoife stayed. She walked out to the thin place, where the white crust had split into plates, and stood there with her hands in her pockets. Lanying came after a while, limping, and stood beside her. Neither of them mentioned the date. Aoife handed her the clipboard and the pen, and Lanying wrote one more line at the bottom of the column, below the others, in her own hand.

g.passage:
We meet on the promenade at four, Ofelia and I,
the board on the bench between us, the gulls on the rail.
Thirty years she has opened with the same pawn.
Thirty years I have answered it badly on purpose
so she can say, as she likes to say, Bartolo, you learn nothing.

This spring her hand shakes when she lifts the queen.
I do not look. I study the harbor, the cranes, a red ship.
Her move, when it comes, is ______,
and I answer as if it were the old one,
the same bad answer, the same small loss.
She says my line. I nod. The tide goes out
the way it has gone out every afternoon in Valparaiso,

g.passage: Two iced coffees, condensed milk at the bottom, a paper straw already going soft: Arman ordered for both of them without asking, as he had every morning that month. The cafe at the Chiang Mai station faced platform two, and Kiet sat facing it too, his bag between his feet, the letter from the boarding school in Bangkok folded into quarters in his shirt pocket. Arman talked about the timetable. The 8:30 was usually late; the 9:10 had a better carriage; the seats on the left got the morning sun until Lampang. He described the vendors who would come through with sticky rice, and which ones to avoid. He described the toilets. Kiet said yes, thank you, he knew. Arman drank his coffee. When the 8:30 was announced, on time, he stood, picked up Kiet's bag before Kiet could reach it, carried it to the carriage door, handed it up, and stayed on the platform with his hands in his pockets until the train had passed the signal box.
